intro: Four different quantities get called "the risk" in this literature and they are not the same: whether the event happens at all; whether it kills more than a tenth of humanity in five years (a global catastrophe); whether the population falls below five thousand (extinction); and whether humanity's long-term potential is destroyed by any route including permanent dystopia (an existential catastrophe, which is a strictly larger event set). The tournament that produced two of the rows below explicitly rejected the fourth as unresolvable. Comparing across them without saying which is which is the commonest error in the field, so this table says which each source measured, and over what horizon.
survivalNote: The dashed lines are published estimates, not model output. They sit at different horizons and measure different events — Ord's is existential catastrophe by 2120, the tournament figures are extinction by 2100 — so read them as landmarks rather than as a target the curve should hit.

commentary: Ord's rows do not sum to his total. Adding the anthropogenic ones naively gives about 1 in 5.3 against a stated 1 in 6, because — as he says — the figures are rounded to the nearest factor of ten. There is a warning in that for this page specifically: a model that treats hazards as independent and multiplies survival probabilities across them will overshoot. This one does exactly that, and the overshoot is real.
Ord's horizon is 2121, not 2100. Comparing his 1 in 6 against a by-2100 figure silently adds twenty years of hazard, which is why the horizon control above offers 2120 as well.

The 2008 survey's 19% is the highest number on this page and the weakest. Its own opening sentence calls it an informal survey circulated among participants at a conference on catastrophic risk — a room selected for believing the subject matters — and the authors add that the results should be taken with a grain of salt. It is on the table because leaving it off would be curating the evidence.

The two tournament rows are the most interesting disagreement here. Superforecasters and domain experts were made to argue with each other at length, with incentives to persuade, and came away differing by roughly a factor of six on total extinction and a factor of eight on AI specifically. Persuasion did not converge them. That is not noise to be averaged away — it is the state of knowledge, and the 'whose prior' control lets you run either one.
